Introduction:
Preterm birth (PTB)—delivery before 37 completed weeks of gestation, with a global prevalence of 10.6%—is the leading cause of death in children who are <5 years old [ 1 ]. This condition is also a common reason for newborn hospital admissions due to severe complications and is associated with poor health in childhood and adulthood [ 2 ].

Tens of studies report associations of ambient temperature with PTB by using various epidemiological study designs, exposure measures, and exposure periods. Most of these studies have examined short-term exposures only. For example, several time series studies found that immediate exposure to high temperature on the day of birth or a few days before is associated with PTB [ 3–7 ]. Similarly, a handful of case-crossover studies observed that exposure to heat during the week before birth is related to PTB [ 8–11 ]. In addition, several cohort studies reported positive associations between high temperatures or heatwaves in the week before birth and PTB [ 12–18 ]. While this literature generally demonstrates positive associations for acute exposures, its main limitation is the lack of consideration of effects in earlier gestation weeks.

Other cohort studies have examined longer-term exposures, such as the last month before birth, the entire pregnancy average, and trimester-specific exposures [ 19–26 ]. Most of these studies fitted separate models for each exposure period. However, as temperatures in different periods during pregnancy are highly correlated, exposure in one period might confound the association between exposure in another period and PTB [ 27 ].

Distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs) add different exposure periods (lags) to the model while addressing their collinearity by using a lag–response function [ 28 ]. To date, only three cohort studies have examined associations between temperature and PTB by using DLNMs and survival analysis [ 29–31 ]. Adapting DLNMs to prenatal exposures creates a challenge due to varying gestational lengths. A study in France used two exposure periods in a DLNM: the last 30 days of pregnancy and 26 weeks after conception, to avoid this issue [ 29 ]. While innovative, this approach mixes the reference times of the exposure, as some exposures are defined by gestation week, while other exposures in the same model are determined by the birth date. Moreover, some of these exposure periods overlap for some of the pregnancies. This limits the interpretation of critical periods by gestation weeks. A study in Sweden defined exposure weeks backward from the week of birth, which leads to a similar limitation [ 30 ].

DLNMs can also estimate associations of cumulative exposures throughout pregnancy, calculated for scenarios of fixed exposure relative to another fixed reference exposure. However, such scenarios are unrealistic for most climates, in which temperatures vary throughout pregnancy due to seasonality.

Few studies also examined the effect modification by socioeconomic status (SES) [ 3 , 7 , 11 , 14 , 17 , 22 ], race [ 4 , 8 ], or body mass index (BMI) [ 8 , 32 ], with inconsistent results. The effect of ambient temperature on very early, early, or late PTB may also be different. Several studies stratified the associations by the timing of PTB and yielded incongruent results [ 5 , 6 , 10 , 11 , 16 , 18 , 23 , 24 ]. However, stratifying by gestational age groups may induce a collider bias [ 33 ] and an alternative methodological approach may be pursued.

In this study, we aimed to examine the critical temperature exposure periods for PTB by using DLNMs and survival analysis in an innovative methodological approach. This enabled us to differentiate between PTB during various phases of pregnancy, estimate associations with realistic exposure scenarios throughout pregnancy, and examine vulnerable groups in Southern Israel by using a historical cohort of ∼130 000 births.
Methods:
### Study design and study population

We employed a historical cohort design utilizing electronic health records of members of Clalit Health Services (henceforth: Clalit), the largest health maintenance organization in Israel, who gave birth at Soroka University Medical Centre in Be’er Sheva. Soroka is the only tertiary-level hospital in Southern Israel and ∼70% of the population in that area are Clalit members [ 34 ]. We obtained data on all live births that occurred at Soroka between 1 January 2005 and 31 December 2019 ( n =
 157 478) and had 131 599 births available for analysis after exclusions (see Supplementary Figure S1 for a complete description of the exclusions).

### Outcome definition

Gestational age at delivery was estimated at the hospital by using the last menstrual period (LMP) date (when available) and ultrasonography. PTB was defined as a birth occurring before 37 completed gestation weeks and categorized into four groups: <28, 28–31, 32–33, and 34–36 completed weeks [ 1 , 35 ].

### Exposure assessment

We assessed ambient temperature with a spatiotemporal model—an ensemble of machine-learning models of random forest, extreme gradient boosting, and generalized additive models [ 36 ]. Its estimates are based on satellite measurements, observations from weather stations, and reanalysis of synoptic conditions. The model performs well with an overall root mean square error of 0.3°C, providing hourly temperature estimates for a grid of 1 km × 1 km for Israel for the study period [ 36 ].

The Clalit database provided coordinates for residential addresses when available. As noted above, we excluded all addresses outside the southern district ( n =
 3558; 2.4%), as they might have been outdated. For other addresses, the geocoding quality and exposure assignment are described in Supplementary Table S1 . Further details on the exposure assessment are found in the Supplementary Material .

### Covariates

We drew a directed acyclic graph (DAG) [ 37 ] showing our assumptions about the causal relationships among the study variables to determine the minimal set of variables to be conditioned to eliminate bias and confounding ( Fig. 1a ). According to the analysis of the DAG using DAGitty [ 38 ], the minimal set of variables to be adjusted for was: SES, ethnicity, locality, seasonality, and air pollution ( Fig. 1b ). As the confounding effects of air pollution and locality on other associations of temperature and pregnancy outcomes in the region seemed negligible in prior studies, we adjusted for these variables only in sensitivity analyses.

We examined effect modification by ethnicity (Arab/Jewish), infant sex, area-level SES, and pre-pregnancy BMI. Area-level SES was based on census-level small-statistical-area classification from the Israel Central Bureau of Statistics [ 39 ]. We estimated pre-pregnancy BMI by the median of height measurements and the last weight measurement within 2 years prior to the pregnancy until the first month of the pregnancy.

### Statistical analyses

We fitted Cox proportional-hazards models with time-dependent covariates integrated with a DLNM [ 28 , 40 ]. We utilized gestation weeks as the time and birth as the event to estimate how the conditional associations between the mean weekly temperature and PTB varied throughout gestation. Further details about the model can be found in the Supplementary Material .

Formula 1 specifies the primary model equation for the hazard function λ i ( t ) ⁠ , where C i represents time-independent covariates, such as SES and ethnicity, Z i ( t ) represents time-dependent covariates (sine and cosine of the week of the year for each gestation week, adjusting for seasonality), and X i represents the time-dependent exposures (i.e. weekly temperature) added into the model in a cross-basis function s x ( X i , t ; β x ) ⁠ . λ 0 ( t ) is the baseline hazard function and β c ⁠ , β z ⁠ , and β x are the other Cox model parameters with respect to the time-independent covariates C i ⁠ , time-dependent covariates Z i ( t ) ⁠ , and the cross-basis functions, respectively [ 41 ]. The causal structure assumed for the time-dependent covariates and exposures is demonstrated by the schematic DAG in Supplementary Figure S2 . Robust standard errors were used to account for the dependency between pregnancies of the same mother [ 42 ].

To examine whether the association of exposure in a specific gestation week with PTB changes for different delivery weeks, we used an extension of the previous Cox model, which enables time-dependent coefficients differing by PTB groups based on gestational age at delivery (as defined above) without stratifying the model (see Supplementary Material for technical details) [ 40 ].

In addition, we used the primary model to examine the associations of exposure to minimum (instead of mean) temperature with the risk of PTB. We also added possible effect modifiers to the primary models as interaction terms, calculated P -values for interaction using likelihood ratio tests, and stratified models by these modifiers. In sensitivity analyses, we further adjusted our models for air pollution by using weekly PM 2.5 concentrations and locality. We also fitted a model without seasonality covariates. All analyses were performed in R, version 4.3.1 [ 43 ], using the survival [ 42 ] and dlnm [ 28 ] packages.

### Risk estimation by temperature trajectories

To demonstrate the implications of our results for the risk of PTB by different realistic exposure trajectories throughout pregnancy, we estimated the survival probability by Week 37: S ( t = 37 ) ⁠ . For this estimation, we used 37 weeks of exposure and covariates of each pregnancy according to LMP date and residential address, regardless of the actual date of birth. We then estimated the cumulative PTB risk by using 1 – S ( t = 37 ) ⁠ , i.e. the probability of not completing 37 gestational weeks.

For the current dataset, the seasonal factor plays a major role in determining the exposure estimated by the spatiotemporal model: by using a univariate linear regression model, we found that 86% of the variability in weekly temperature can be explained by the LMP month. Therefore, we calculated the average estimated PTB risk by using the LMP month. Finally, we estimated the relative risks for each LMP month by dividing the average risk in each month by the risk of the lowest average risk (March). The 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated by bootstrapping using 500 samples with replacement. A formal description of this approach can be found in the Supplementary Material .
Results:
In our cohort of 131 599 deliveries in Southern Israel, the prevalence of PTB was 7%. More than half of the study population were Bedouin-Arab and nearly half of the mothers with available pre-pregnancy BMI data were overweight or obese ( Table 1 ). Supplementary Figure S3 illustrates the exposure distribution, Supplementary Figure S4 presents its spatial distribution, and Supplementary Figure S5 demonstrates the correlation structure among exposure weeks of gestation. The proportions of Arabs and mothers with lower SES were higher in the lower-temperature quintiles ( Supplementary Table S2 ) and Arabs comprised the majority in the first and second SES quartiles ( Supplementary Table S3 ).

Temperature exposures in gestation Weeks 1–28 were not associated with PTB. However, higher temperatures during the third trimester were associated with a higher risk of early delivery. For example, exposure to 31°C (99th percentile) in Week 29 presented an hazard ratio (HR) of 1.02 (95% CI: 1.00–1.03) with PTB compared with the minimum-risk temperature (16°C). Similarly, exposures to 31°C in Weeks 30–37 were associated with PTB, with increasing strength towards the end of the third trimester. The strongest association was for exposure during Week 37 (HR= 1.04, 95% CI: 1.01–1.07; Fig. 2 ). There were no major differences in associations by groups of PTB severity ( Supplementary Figures S6–S9 ).

We did not find any interaction with ethnicity and SES ( P for interaction = 0.18 and 0.84, respectively). Weekly associations were slightly stronger in female than male fetuses ( P for interaction < 0.001; Supplementary Figure S10 ). In addition, associations were somewhat different in women with pre-pregnancy underweight or overweight, but the pattern of difference was unclear ( P for interaction <0.001; Supplementary Figure S11 ). Cancelling the seasonality adjustment or adding adjustments for PM 2.5 and locality did not materially change the results ( Supplementary Figures S12–S14 ). Associations with minimum (instead of mean) daily temperature were also similar ( Supplementary Figure S15 ).

The average estimated risk of PTB across exposure trajectories defined by the LMP month displayed a clear seasonal pattern, with the lowest risk estimated for pregnancies with LMP between February and April and the highest risk for those with LMP during the autumn ( Fig. 3 , top). The average estimated risk by LMP month varied between 6.5% and 7.6% for pregnancies with LMP in March and October, respectively, translated into a relative risk of 1.17 with a 95% CI of 1.07–1.27 ( Fig. 3 , middle; Supplementary Table S4 ). Exposure trajectories for pregnancies starting in the autumn also included the highest temperatures during Weeks 33–37 of gestation ( Fig. 3 , bottom).
Discussion:
In this cohort of >130 000 singleton live births in Southern Israel, we examined the critical periods of and vulnerable groups to the associations between temperature and PTB. Exposures to high temperatures during gestation Weeks 29–37 were associated with an increased risk of PTB, with stronger associations in females. Pregnancies starting in the autumn were exposed to the highest temperatures in Weeks 33–37 and had the highest estimated PTB risk.

Our findings align with most literature showing an association between heat and PTB. For example, cohort studies in Australia, the USA, Israel, and China found that heat in the week before birth was associated with PTB, with HRs ranging from 1.02 to 2.00 [ 12 , 13 , 15 , 16 ]. However, a few studies found no association with heat exposure in the last week of pregnancy [ 21 , 24 , 30 ] and a time-series study from China found a negative association [ 44 ]. While the associations that we found in the final weeks of the PTB risk period support the associations of acute exposures in these studies, our findings are not fully comparable due to different definitions of the exposure windows. Our exposures were defined by gestation week, while theirs were determined by the date of birth, which does not correspond to a specific gestation week. Fetuses go through different physiological stages in each gestation week and examining exposures by gestation weeks—instead of relative to birth date—enables the detection of critical periods and an understanding of biological mechanisms.

Some cohort studies investigating exposures throughout gestation found similar associations in later stages of pregnancy. For example, a cohort study in Australia fitted separate Cox models for temperature in each trimester and found positive associations for extreme heat and cold only in the third trimester [ 26 ]. However, some found associations in the earlier stages, such as a Korean cohort that demonstrated positive associations for heatwaves in the first and second trimesters [ 19 ]. Another study from China found the strongest associations for the average exposure in Weeks 8–14 [ 25 ]. While our results partly overlap with those of these studies, it is challenging to draw comparisons due to the different exposure windows. More importantly, these studies examined each exposure window in a separate model, raising concern that some associations were confounded by exposure in other gestation weeks.

Three studies used a Cox model with a DLNM. One study in China found that high temperatures in Weeks 4–8 and 22–27 were associated with increased PTB risk, while the same exposure during Weeks 10–20 was associated with decreased risk [ 31 ]. A similar study in France found positive associations for heat in Weeks 3–7 and 22–28 for minimum temperatures but not for mean temperatures [ 29 ]. A study in Sweden did not find clear associations, possibly explained by the different climates [ 30 ].

Several studies examined whether the associations vary according to the timing of the PTB by stratifying their analyses by gestational age categories, with contradictory findings [ 5 , 10 , 11 , 16 , 18 , 23 , 24 ]. Using a new statistical approach, we observed no major difference in associations, consistently with an American time-series study that examined the issue [ 6 ]. In addition, we did not observe any interaction with ethnicity or SES, despite the differences in living conditions between Jews and Arabs and among SES strata in Southern Israel.

Consistently with our findings, most studies reported stronger associations for female fetuses [ 5 , 10 , 16 ], whereas a case-crossover study in the USA found the opposite [ 11 ] and a few other studies did not detect any interaction [ 6 , 13 , 22 ]. Although male fetuses are at higher risk of PTB [ 45 ], heat-related PTB may be more prominent in female fetuses. The unclear interaction pattern with BMI could be due to a small sample size in subgroups or a selection bias, as BMI was missing for 63% of our population.

The weekly associations that we reported as HRs should not be interpreted as causal effects. Although HRs are standard association measures for Cox models, they suffer from an inherent collider bias due to the conditioning on survival in each follow-up step [ 46 , 47 ]. To partially overcome the limited interpretation of our results, we further estimated cumulative PTB risk for realistic exposure scenarios—a method that does not suffer from the limitations of HRs [ 46 ]. However, defining a causal estimand in this context is more challenging. It is beyond the scope of this work, as it involves the debatable possibility of intervening in temperature exposure.

Examining the time-varying temperature across pregnancy as seasonal exposure trajectories defined by LMP month and comparing the risk by these trajectories is a new methodological approach presented in this work. Although the distribution of higher temperatures at the end of the preterm risk period by the LMP month does not entirely align with the estimated PTB risk, the overlap for the months in autumn demonstrates the relationship between exposure and risk of PTB in our models. While the magnitude of the weekly associations is limited to HRs of 1.04, the cumulative associations throughout pregnancy, when comparing LMP months, are approximately 4-fold higher. Considering also the high incidence of PTB and the abundant exposure—predicted to increase with climate change—emphasizes the importance of our findings.

The main strength of our study was that we used state-of-the-art statistical methods and further developed them. First, we used Cox models with time-dependent covariates integrated with a DLNM and improved these models to fit prenatal exposures by addressing the issue of differing pregnancy lengths. Second, we applied a new approach to demonstrate the predictions of the model for realistic cumulative exposure trajectories. Third, we used time-dependent coefficients to determine whether the associations varied by follow-up time, avoiding exclusion or stratification by gestational age that may have led to collider bias [ 33 ]. Fourth, we introduced adjustment for seasonality as a time-varying covariate and found through a sensitivity analysis that seasonality was not an actual confounder in our study.

Our study had limitations as well. Exposure was based on residential addresses, creating some exposure error. However, this error was likely to be non-differential and therefore more likely to bias the associations to the null. We also lacked data on indoor temperatures, air-conditioner use, or other ways to change personal exposure. Instead, our exposure estimate was a proxy for personal exposure, creating another source of non-differential error [ 48 ]. However, proxy measurements have the methodological advantage of not being prone to confounding by personal behaviors [ 48 ]. Additionally, we only had data on live births, which are prone to live-birth bias [ 49 ].

In summary, our findings highlight the late weeks of the third trimester as the critical window concerning heat and PTB. Future research on biological mechanisms can focus on the possible effects of heat in the later stages of fetal development. In addition, this study underlines the need for future studies to consider the role of seasonality thoroughly.
